Sponsor: Lian Li O11D Evo RGB on Amazon https://geni.us/B3OD
AMD's Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB and 8GB GPUs launch tomorrow. Our review of the AMD RX 9060 XT 16GB tests the card versus the NVIDIA RTX 5060, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, prior AMD RX 7700 XT, 6600 XT, and similar GPUs, and even the GTX 1060 6GB. A large portion of the initial commentary focuses on what we believe to be misleading statements by AMD that reshape the conversation about what is acceptable for a $300 GPU in 2025. AMD, like NVIDIA, is taking advantage of consumers more aggressively than we've seen in the past; this is unfortunate, seeing as the company initially showed some self awareness with the RX 9070 XT and RX 9070 launch. Still, we focus on benchmarks and compare the new GPU to alternatives on the market and as an upgrade option. We also show the VRAM limitation issues for 8GB cards, though we aren't testing the 9060 XT 8GB model today (that'll be in a separate piece; we're not sure when yet, as we want to add some extra depth).

I was a nvidia fan for a long time.... up until 5 days ago when my nephew bought a 5060 and asked me to install it in his B450 motherboard with a ryzen 5 in it.   Now call me crazy but usually a card upgrade is pretty straight forward,  uninstall previous drivers, turn off system, pull out old card, put in new card, turn on system, install drivers, and go back to gaming.    Yea,  that didn't happen with the 5060. Installed card,  installed drivers, windows 10 crashes,  restart sends into black loop of hell.   Go into safe mode, uninstall drivers, system functions like normal.  Rinse and repeat.   Look online and alot of other people having similar problems with not only the 5060, but ALL the 5000 series and certain motherboard chipsets.    

5 hours later after a bios update, windows updates, trying things like switching pcie to gen 3 from gen 4, trying different drivers and a few other recommendations...... still doesn't work.   

Took it back, got a 9060 xt 16gb, plugged it in, installed adrenaline drivers, off to the races.   

I don't know what the hell nvidia is thinking but if they continue on this path they're going to lose customers.   

Normal people aren't going to troubleshoot for 4 hours trying to figure out why their system went crazy, they just want something that works and something as minimalistic as a video card upgrade shouldn't cause that kind of grief for people.

comments.text: The Frank Azor public statement is a bit tongue-in-cheek corpo-speek for investors, shareholders, and zealous fans. It's the unfortunate language we all learn at these levels in companies. He's not wrong in any way except one. The problem, and only objective problem, is that an 8GB version eats at potential product availability for the 16GB version. You would also be forgiven for thinking AMD is deploying an 8GB version to copycat Nvidia. The flaw in that is that these product stacks are R&D'ed years prior to launch. At most they can change naming schemes prior to launch, and that's it. The 8GB version production cost is likely at most $10 less than the 16GB version, but will get market priced about $50 less. This means AMD and their partners make LESS profit from this version. Ultimately it falls on the customer to know and understand the difference between the two and choose which to purchase. If you think it's hard for customers to know what they are getting from their graphics card purchases, I'ld like to show you a line-up of laptops in their original boxes. See if you can tell the differences at a glance. But hey, maybe you and/or HWUB Steve can bring some unforeseen objective argument to the table that really justifies this hatred for 8GB/16GB variants of the exact same product. comments.text:
I'm pretty sure "no compromise" in that paragraph is about the 16 GB model (i.e., you get more VRAM if you play games that need it while getting the same GPU). The 8 GB model is the one with a "compromise" (i.e., meant only for 1080p "e-sports" - read Counter-strike), in exchange for a lower price. AMD probably makes about the same on both models, assuming the GPU itself is exactly the same; the price difference will be up to the card manufacturers, how much the VRAM costs, and how much they save in manufacturing.

I think you're so used to Nvidia completely controlling its AIBs that you assume AMD can do the same. They can't; they represent less than 20% of the discrete GPU market. Prices and models are going to be determined (or at least heavily influenced) by the card manufacturers.

comments.text:
"They decide what game requirements are. Nothing will change until new console generations."
Except that we are already seeing the shift away from these things. Frame gen is becoming normalized and the new Doom among others are the first steps in normalizing mandatory ray tracing. These are games that are coming out while those GPUs and resolutions still dominate. 
The issue is that there is a relationship between developers and hardware manufacturers. Large developers make large hardware orders. So they are incentivized to add in the shiny new hardware features in order to cut deals on hardware purchases. This regardless of where the bulk of their playerbase is because they know that they can use their game to up sell people on hardware upgrades. It's not an accident that Monster Hunter Wilds game codes were "free" parts of several promotions for the current crop of GPUs.

There are more factors involved here than simply what hardware people have.

comments.text:
The thing I hate most about this "8GB is enough for 1080p" is that it's a bunk argument to begin with. It assumes that resolution is the end all be all of keeping within a VRAM buffer. 1080p in 2025 is not the same as 1080p in 2016 when the 1060 came out. Many many options are just as or more demanding on VRAM in modern games as resolution. If a game is running at the same settings and you only change the resolution to 1440p or 4k the difference isn't going to be 8gb, it's going to be 2-4gb. Which is why 12gb runs 1080p games flawlessly regardless of settings while 8gb requires multiple compromises. 

This is also going to get worse because, as we've seen in the last 8 months or so, more and more games are coming out without the option to fully disable RT effects. RT gobbles up VRAM far worse than resolution does. This is only going to get more and more common with each release as devs streamline their workload to stop supplying two bespoke lighting solutions for every title. I mean RT's been around for 6 years, the transition has to happen at some point. Whether hardware is ready or not doesn't mean squat to publishers because they really don't care if a game runs well or not. Turn on DLSS or FSR if you want 30 fps is all they'll say.  

Also, the focus on "esports titles" is also BS. A toaster can run those in excess of 100 FPS at 1080p. You don't need a new card for that. Literally any video card made since 2019 can blast through Esports games. It's a nonsense talking point. Hell, if you buy a now nearly 10 year old 1080ti you'd tear through every single esports title and you'd get 11gb of ram to boot. The Esports gamer doesn't need to upgrade unless they are running something incredibly low end. What would these 8gb cards even be an upgrade from? They run about just as well as 3060ti from 4 years ago and that had a 12gb model. They'd be better off buying one of those used. Or you know, consoles and phones also have most esports titles and run them just fine because, again, a toaster can run them.

So, this entire conversation comes immediately from a place of dishonesty and hyper focuses on something that's not as relevant as they'd like you to think (resolution) or are already completely irrelevant (esports discussion) and will become more and more irrelevant going forward. I hate all of it, the whole conversation is crap and everyone just goes along with the faulty framing AMD/Nvidia is pushing for justifying 8gb in 2025.

comments.text:
I have a dual 22" 1080p 75 Hz setup. I'm a modest gamer, who plays Stellaris, JRPGs and other non-esport genres (maybe some fighters which are framelocked to 60 fps). I don't see the benefit of going 1440p, because I have more than enough games where 720p-1080p remains a sweet spot where I don't need to juggle with resolutions and UI scaling, but above them I am required to include intermediary layers like cnc-ddraw to downsample the game's output resolution for an upscaling without relying on legacy fullscreen affecting the other monitor. Also, 22"-24" is the sweet spot for me, I hate working with bigger monitors. I enjoy using my 14" 1080p without any UI upscaling, but I hate dealing with all those 26"+ monstrosities where I require head movement to see both edges of the active monitor's fullscreen content.

Also keep in mind that 720p/1080p basically came from the movie industry. The last dominating 4:3 gaming resolution was 1024x768, despite the fact that 1280x1024 was widely available at the dawn of the widescreen, basically floating in the same role of today's 1440p. If the GPUs would be able to run 4k on popular games, I'm pretty sure 1440p would even be skipped for game optimization and whatnot.

That's really not even a relevant thing. The entire argument that 8gb is fine at 1080p is bunk anyway. Resolution is not the end all be all of keeping within a VRAM buffer in 2025. If you apply the same settings on a game and change the resolution from 1080 to 1440 to 4k you aren't going to see more than a 2-4gb difference AT MOST. Many many other settings in modern games are just as impactful on VRAM as resolution is. On modern AAA releases you WILL have to compromise somewhere on an 8gb card regardless of resolution otherwise you will be smacking into that 8gb. That's only going to get worse with each passing month and each new game that stops giving you the option of turning off RT. RT is much MUCH heavier on VRAM than resolution and more and more games are going to be shipping without a toggle for it going forward. a year or two from now 8gb cards will basically be forced to use FSR/DLSS at performance at 1080p with lowered settings just to function. Resulting in a blurry ugly experience. 

This whole conversation is a smokescreen to justify selling these compromised misleading models to unsuspecting and less informed customers. It's gross.

comments.text: ​@TheVanillatech The push for higher margins on lower end cards is certainly a thing but you also have to deal with the fact that Moore's law is basically dead. The ability to constantly offer better performance at a lower cost is running up against basic physics at this point. You can still make big performance gains at the high end by spamming transistors and upping power budgets and making things more expensive, but that's not trickling down to the mid range much and the low end has basically been replaced by IGPUs. In the console space, where specs stay static for 5-10 years, developers have gotten pretty good at making great games despite hardware stagnation. In the PC space, they really haven't and probably never will. The PC market has proven less tolerant of massively expensive games, meaning that prices on Steam, etc still drop after launch in a way that they just don't on consoles anymore. That means that game companies are incentivized to push people towards console releases.
